meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Good artists copy; great artists steal'?
meta.ogDescription: Steve Jobs made it famous and pinned it on Picasso — but no evidence supports Picasso. The line traces to T.S. Eliot (1920). Here's the paper trail.

answer.label: Not Picasso — a line Steve Jobs made famous
answer.authorDates: 1888–1965 · American-British poet & critic; wrote the earliest documented form
answer.sourceLine: Steve Jobs really did say “Good artists copy; great artists steal” — on camera in the 1996 documentary Triumph of the Nerds — but he credited Pablo Picasso, and Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Picasso ever said it. The dictum’s earliest documented form is T. S. Eliot’s 1920 line “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” with an 1892 precursor. The exact “artists” wording Jobs used cannot be pinned to Picasso or any single author.

source.heading: The paper trail behind the line
source.excerpt: Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal; bad poets deface what they take, and good poets make it into something better, or at least something different.
trail: The authoritative anchor: Quote Investigator reports it “has not yet located substantive evidence for the attribution to Picasso,” and traces the saying to T. S. Eliot (1920) with an 1892 precursor by W. H. Davenport Adams.
Wikiquote files the Picasso attribution under Misattributed, noting Jobs is “(mis)quoting Pablo Picasso” and that the sayings “may well originate in T. S. Eliot’s dictum.”
Eliot’s original: “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” from “Philip Massinger” in The Sacred Wood (1920).
Per QI, the “artists” variant surfaces only by 1959 (Marvin Magalaner: “Immature artists borrow; mature artists steal”) — long after the poets version and with no Picasso trail.
source.excerptNote: T. S. Eliot’s 1920 dictum — the earliest documented form of the idea. The compressed “Good artists copy; great artists steal” is a much later paraphrase that Steve Jobs pinned on Picasso.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented ancestor — T. S. Eliot’s 1920 line — is itself public domain (first published before 1931). But the exact modern wording “Good artists copy; great artists steal” has no pinned first publication: it is a compressed paraphrase Steve Jobs popularized in 1996 while crediting Picasso, and no source ties that exact phrasing to Picasso or any single author. Its provenance is therefore uncertain.

author.name: T. S. Eliot
author.heading: About T. S. Eliot
author.bio: Thomas Stearns Eliot was a poet, critic, and playwright whose criticism reshaped how the English-speaking world read poetry. In his 1920 essay collection The Sacred Wood, discussing the dramatist Philip Massinger, he coined the memorable formula that a mature poet does not merely imitate but steals — the earliest documented ancestor of the line later attached to Picasso and popularized by Steve Jobs.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it?
misattribution.intro: This line is a double misattribution: pinned on Picasso by the man who made it famous, and often credited to Steve Jobs himself.

items.why: Steve Jobs credited Picasso, but Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Picasso ever said it, and Wikiquote lists it as misattributed.
Jobs genuinely said it — in the 1996 documentary Triumph of the Nerds — but he explicitly attributed it to Picasso, so he is the popularizer of a much older idea, not its originator.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented form is T. S. Eliot’s 1920 “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” itself echoing an 1892 line by W. H. Davenport Adams — the exact “good artists / great artists” wording is a later paraphrase with no verified single author.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The saying became gospel in tech and design culture largely because of Steve Jobs, who invoked it to justify Apple’s borrowing of ideas — from Xerox PARC’s graphical interface to typography. Crediting Picasso gave a scrappy act of appropriation the blessing of high-art genius.

But the genealogy runs through literary criticism, not painting. Eliot’s point was precise: weak borrowers merely imitate, while great ones absorb what they take and transform it into something wholly their own — a far more demanding claim than “stealing is fine.”
context.pull: Jobs really said it — but he was quoting a Picasso who never said it.
